title: Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes
blurb: Explain the chromosome 15 imprinting pair, plan lawful food security in Prader-Willi syndrome, and meet the seizure and communication needs of Angelman syndrome.
question: Leah, 30, has Prader-Willi syndrome and is admitted to a medical ward with cellulitis of her leg after skin picking. A snack trolley passes the bay several times a day. What should the nurse put in place?

teach.body: Prader-Willi and Angelman syndromes both involve the same small region of chromosome 15 (15q11-q13). In this region, some genes work only from the copy inherited from one parent: this is genomic imprinting. Losing the father's working genes causes Prader-Willi syndrome; losing the mother's working UBE3A gene causes Angelman syndrome. In plain English: which parent's copy is missing decides which syndrome develops.

teach.caption: UPD (uniparental disomy): both copies come from one parent. Two maternal copies means no paternal genes: Prader-Willi.
Both: sleep problems. Frequency: PWS 1 in 10,000–30,000; Angelman 1 in 12,000–20,000.

items.label: Floppy, weak suck, poor feeding and growth

teach.caption: The feeding problem flips: from too little in infancy to uncontrollable hunger later.

teach.body: Hyperphagia is not greed and cannot be controlled by willpower. A secure food environment (structured meals, food stored out of reach) protects health, but locking food away restricts the person and often their housemates. If the person has capacity and agrees, record their consent. If capacity is in doubt, assess it for that decision; if they lack it, any restriction must be in their best interests and the less restrictive option considered, with regular review.

Why
Nursing action
teach.caption: NICE NG54 1.7.4 names behavioural phenotypes such as psychosis in Prader-Willi syndrome.

teach.h: Nursing a person with Angelman syndrome
teach.body: Severe speech impairment is core: offer signs, symbols, objects or a communication aid alongside speech. Epilepsy is common, so a seizure plan is essential. Ataxia and balance problems increase falls risk. Sleep problems affect the whole family. A happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter is part of the syndrome, so laughter is not evidence of comfort: assess pain using the person's known cues.

items.label: Prader-Willi: deletion on the father's chromosome 15
Angelman: deletion on the mother's chromosome 15

teach.h: Scenario: Leah on the medical ward
teach.body: The nurse contacts Leah's support team for her existing food plan and agrees a ward version with Leah: set mealtimes, catering told, snacks and visitors' food kept out of her bay as her plan allows. Her consent or best interests record is checked, not assumed. Her wound is treated and skin picking is planned for (keeping hands busy, covering the wound). Blood glucose and weight are monitored. Free access to food on a ward could cause rapid weight gain and choking risk from rushed eating.

teach.text: Don't swap the parents: Prader-Willi = PATERNAL loss (P for P). Angelman = MATERNAL UBE3A loss. And maternal UPD causes Prader-Willi, because two maternal copies mean no paternal genes.

items: Chromosome 15q11-q13 imprinting: paternal loss = Prader-Willi; maternal UBE3A loss = Angelman.
Prader-Willi: floppy, poor feeding in infancy, then hyperphagia, obesity, type 2 diabetes, skin picking.
Food restriction needs consent or a best interests decision, least restrictive, reviewed.
Angelman: severe LD, minimal speech, ataxia, epilepsy, frequent laughter, sleep problems.
Laughter in Angelman does not rule out pain.

summary: You can now explain how imprinting on chromosome 15 produces Prader-Willi or Angelman syndrome, recognise their features, and plan care: lawful food security, weight and diabetes monitoring in Prader-Willi, and communication, seizure and pain assessment in Angelman.

A.q: A student asks which set of features is most typical of Angelman syndrome. Which is correct?
options: Extreme hunger, short stature and skin picking
Severe learning disability, ataxia and frequent laughter
Hand wringing after a period of early regression
Long narrow face, large ears and social anxiety
A.why: Angelman syndrome: severe learning disability, minimal speech, ataxia, epilepsy and a happy excitable manner with frequent laughter.

whyNot.0: These are features of Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyNot.2: Regression with hand wringing is Rett syndrome.
whyNot.3: These are features of fragile X syndrome.

A.q: What is the most common genetic mechanism causing Prader-Willi syndrome?
options: Two copies of chromosome 15 from the mother
A variant in the UBE3A gene from the mother
An extra copy of chromosome 15 in every cell
A deletion on the chromosome 15 from the father
A.why: About 70% of Prader-Willi syndrome is due to a deletion on the paternal chromosome 15; about 25% is maternal uniparental disomy.

whyNot.0: Maternal UPD causes about 25%, not most cases.
whyNot.1: Maternal UBE3A changes cause Angelman syndrome.
whyNot.2: Prader-Willi is a loss of paternal genes, not an extra chromosome.

A.q: Leah, 30, has Prader-Willi syndrome. On admission the nurse sees several open sores on her forearms. Staff at her home say this is long-standing. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Record it as deliberate self-harm and refer to the crisis team
Assume eczema and apply an emollient to the sores twice daily
Recognise skin picking, treat the wounds and plan to reduce it
Cover the sores and continue her usual routine without change
A.why: Skin picking is a recognised feature of Prader-Willi syndrome. The wounds need assessment and treatment, and a plan to reduce picking and infection risk.

whyNot.0: Skin picking in Prader-Willi is a known feature, not a crisis presentation in itself.
whyNot.1: Assuming eczema misses the cause and the infection risk.
whyNot.3: Open sores need assessment and treatment, not just covering.

B.q: NICE NG54 notes that some syndromes carry particular mental health risks. Which pairing does it name?
options: Psychosis in Prader-Willi syndrome
Psychosis in Angelman syndrome
Mania in fragile X syndrome
Dementia in Rett syndrome
B.why: NICE NG54 1.7.4 refers to behavioural phenotypes, including psychosis in Prader-Willi syndrome and anxiety in autism.

whyNot.1: NG54 does not name psychosis in Angelman syndrome.
whyNot.2: NG54 does not name mania in fragile X.
whyNot.3: Early dementia is linked to Down syndrome, not Rett.

B.q: Toby, 9, has Angelman syndrome and is moving to a new school. Which health need is most important to include in his school care plan?
options: Locked food access because of extreme hunger
Yearly thyroid testing throughout his life
A seizure management plan for his epilepsy
Screening for early-onset dementia from 30
B.why: Epilepsy is a core feature of Angelman syndrome, so school staff need a seizure management plan.

whyNot.0: Hyperphagia is a feature of Prader-Willi, not Angelman.
whyNot.1: Lifelong yearly thyroid testing is a Down syndrome priority.
whyNot.3: Early-onset dementia screening is linked to Down syndrome.

B.q: Megan, 27, has Prader-Willi syndrome and capacity to decide about her food. She asks staff to keep her own food cupboard locked to help her manage her hunger. What should staff do?
options: Lock it under a best interests decision made by the team
Agree the plan with her consent, record it and review it
Decline, as locking food is not allowed in supported living
Apply to the Court of Protection before locking it
B.why: Megan has capacity and is asking for the support. Her consent is the lawful basis; staff record the agreement and review it with her.

whyNot.0: Best interests decisions apply when a person lacks capacity; Megan has capacity and consents.
whyNot.2: A consented, person-led plan can be lawful in supported living.
whyNot.3: No court application is needed when a person with capacity consents.

C.q: Leah, 30, has Prader-Willi syndrome and an agreed food plan at home. She is admitted to a medical ward where a snack trolley passes several times a day. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Allow free access to the snack trolley to avoid distress
Agree a ward food plan with Leah and her support team
Lock the ward kitchen for every patient without discussion
Keep her in her bed space at mealtimes to reduce temptation
C.why: Continuity of her existing plan, agreed with Leah and her support team, keeps her safe and lawful: set mealtimes, catering informed, food kept out of reach as her plan allows.

whyNot.0: Unrestricted access risks rapid weight gain and choking from rushed eating.
whyNot.2: A blanket restriction on all patients is disproportionate and not agreed.
whyNot.3: Confining her is a further restriction that is not part of her agreed plan.

C.q: Ruby, 4, has a severe learning disability, no words, an unsteady gait, seizures and a small head, and laughs often. Testing shows a deletion at 15q11-q13. On which chromosome is the deletion most likely to be?
options: The father's chromosome 15
The mother's X chromosome
The father's chromosome 21
The mother's chromosome 15
C.why: Ruby's features fit Angelman syndrome, caused by loss of the maternal UBE3A gene, most often through a deletion on the mother's chromosome 15.

whyNot.0: A paternal deletion here causes Prader-Willi syndrome.
whyNot.1: The region involved is on chromosome 15, not the X.
whyNot.2: Chromosome 21 is linked to Down syndrome.

C.q: Sam, 22, has Prader-Willi syndrome and lives in supported living. Staff report he has gained 8 kg in three months, is always thirsty and is passing urine often. What should the nurse do?
options: Reduce his portions and recheck his weight next month
Encourage more fluids and record his fluid intake
Arrange a blood glucose check and GP review today
Record it as expected in Prader-Willi syndrome
C.why: Thirst and passing urine often with weight gain suggest type 2 diabetes, a known risk in Prader-Willi syndrome. He needs a glucose check and prompt review.

whyNot.0: Portion changes alone ignore possible diabetes.
whyNot.1: Thirst is a symptom to investigate, not to treat with fluids.
whyNot.3: Accepting it as 'part of the syndrome' is diagnostic overshadowing.

reteach.title: P for Paternal, P for Prader-Willi
reteach.question: Both syndromes come from the same spot on chromosome 15. How can you remember which is which?

blocks.body: Prader-Willi: Paternal genes missing; the person is always hungry. Angelman: the mother's UBE3A missing; the person rarely speaks, often laughs, and may have seizures. The same deletion causes a different syndrome depending on which parent it came from.

blocks.text: Maternal UPD (two copies from mother) causes PRADER-WILLI, because the father's genes are missing.

explain.body: In 15q11-q13 some genes work only from one parent's copy. Missing paternal genes: Prader-Willi. Missing maternal UBE3A: Angelman.

test.q: Two children have the same deletion at 15q11-q13 but different syndromes. What explains this?
options: Which parent the deleted chromosome came from
How large each child's deletion turned out to be
Whether the child is male or female
Whether an extra chromosome 21 is present
test.why: Genomic imprinting: a paternal deletion causes Prader-Willi; a maternal deletion causes Angelman.

whyNot.1: The same deletion gives different syndromes by parent of origin.
whyNot.2: Both syndromes affect males and females.
whyNot.3: Chromosome 21 is unrelated to these syndromes.

explain.body: Infancy: hypotonia, weak suck, poor feeding. Childhood onward: hyperphagia, obesity, type 2 diabetes risk, mild to moderate learning disability, skin picking, short stature, delayed puberty, sleep problems.

test.q: Harper, 6 weeks, has Prader-Willi syndrome and needs help with feeding because of a weak suck. Her parents ask why, when they have read that the syndrome causes overeating. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Overeating starts in the first weeks, so feeds are limited
Feeding is often hard in infancy; extreme hunger comes later
The weak suck shows she has a milder form of the syndrome
Tube feeding is needed because overeating has already begun
test.why: Infants with Prader-Willi syndrome have hypotonia, a weak suck and poor feeding; hyperphagia develops later in childhood.

whyNot.0: Hyperphagia develops later, not in early infancy.
whyNot.2: A weak suck is typical of infancy in the syndrome, not a sign of a milder form.
whyNot.3: Feeding support is for poor feeding, not overeating.

explain.body: Locking food is a restriction. With capacity: the person's consent. Capacity in doubt: assess for this decision. Lacking capacity: best interests, less restrictive option, regular review.

test.q: Callum, 31, has Prader-Willi syndrome and shares a house with two others. The team proposes a padlock on the shared fridge. His capacity to decide about food access is in doubt. What must happen first?
options: Fit the padlock now and review it in a month
Ask his parents to consent to the padlock
Assess his capacity for this specific decision
Ask the housemates to vote on the padlock
test.why: Capacity is assessed for the specific decision. If Callum lacks it, a best interests decision weighs the less restrictive options and the effect on his housemates.

whyNot.0: Restricting first and reviewing later reverses the lawful order.
whyNot.1: Parents cannot consent for an adult without legal authority.
whyNot.3: A vote is not a lawful basis for restricting Callum.

explain.body: Severe learning disability, minimal or no speech, ataxia, epilepsy, small head, frequent laughter and hand-flapping, sleep problems. Use total communication; assess pain by known cues, not by laughter.

test.q: Isaac, 12, has Angelman syndrome. He laughs while his injured ankle is being splinted, and a student nurse says he cannot be in much pain. What is the best response?
options: Agree, as laughter is a reliable sign of comfort
His laughter is part of the syndrome and does not rule out pain
Give analgesia if he stops laughing during the procedure
Ask him to rate his pain on a numerical 0 to 10 scale
test.why: Frequent laughter is a feature of Angelman syndrome; pain should be assessed using his known cues and an observational approach.

whyNot.0: In Angelman syndrome laughter does not indicate comfort.
whyNot.2: Waiting for a change in laughter delays pain relief.
whyNot.3: With minimal speech and a severe learning disability, a numerical scale is unlikely to work.
